SINGLE POINT CHARGE
TWO LIKE CHARGES
TWO OPPOSITE CHARGES (DIPOLE)
MULTIPLE CHARGES (COMPLEX)

A single point charge creates a simple electric field pattern. The field lines radiate outward from a positive charge or inward toward a negative charge, forming a symmetrical pattern around the charge.




This pattern is easy to recognize and serves as the foundation for understanding more complex field arrangements. The strength of the field decreases as you move away from the charge.

PARALLEL PLATE CAPACITOR
VARYING PLATE SEPARATION
ELECTRIC POTENTIAL MAPS
ENERGY STORED

In a parallel plate capacitor, two flat plates are placed close together with a gap between them. When charged, a uniform electric field forms in the space between the plates, and the potential difference (voltage) is the same across any line perpendicular to the plates.




This setup is used to store energy in the electric field. The amount of energy stored depends on the charge on the plates and the voltage between them. Capacitors are found in many electronic devices for this reason.

POLARIZATION IN CONDUCTORS
POLARIZATION IN INSULATORS
ATTRACTION OF NEUTRAL OBJECTS
NO NET CHARGE TRANSFER

When a charged object is brought near a conductor, the free electrons in the conductor shift toward or away from the charged object. This creates regions of positive and negative charge within the conductor, even though the overall object remains neutral.




This separation of charge means that one side of the conductor is attracted to the charged object, leading to a noticeable force. The effect disappears once the charged object is removed, as the electrons return to their original positions.

OPEN CIRCUIT
CLOSED CIRCUIT
SHORT CIRCUIT

An open circuit occurs when there is a break or gap somewhere in the path, such as a switch being turned off or a wire being disconnected.




In an open circuit, no current can flow, so devices like bulbs or motors will not work. For example, a lamp with its switch turned off is an open circuit.

+

Tabs
AMMETER
VOLTMETER

An ammeter is always connected in series with the component whose current you want to measure. This means it becomes part of the main path for current, so all the current flows through it.




For example, if you want to measure the current through a resistor, you place the ammeter directly in line with the resistor. This setup ensures the reading reflects the true current in that part of the circuit.

+

Tabs
ADDING IN SERIES
ADDING IN PARALLEL
EQUIVALENT RESISTANCE FORMULAE

When you add resistors in series, their resistances simply add together. The total resistance increases, making it harder for current to flow through the circuit.




This means that each additional resistor reduces the current for a given voltage, and devices may receive less energy.

An ammeter should always be placed in series with the component whose current you want to measure. This allows the ammeter to measure the exact current flowing through that part of the circuit.




Placing the ammeter in series ensures it becomes part of the current's path, giving an accurate reading without affecting the rest of the circuit.

MOTOR
GENERATOR

A motor takes in electrical energy and converts it into mechanical motion. The key components include a coil, magnets, and a commutator (in some types). When current flows through the coil in a magnetic field, the resulting force causes the coil to spin, producing useful work.




Motors are found in devices like electric cars, fans, and washing machines. They are essential for any application where electricity is used to create movement or perform mechanical tasks.

ELECTROMAGNETIC CRANE
ELECTRIC GENERATOR
MAGNETIC BRAKING SYSTEM
DYNAMIC MICROPHONE

An electromagnetic crane uses a powerful coil and iron core to create a strong magnetic field that can lift heavy metal objects. The strength depends on the number of coil turns, the current, and the core material.




Designers must balance lifting power with safety, cost, and heating. Too much current can cause overheating, while too few turns may not lift enough weight. Engineers often test and tweak these variables for the best results.
